Size and shape scores for many correlated traits

Source: R/size_shape.R
size_shape.Rd

Rewrites a set of correlated traits as log size plus orthogonal shape axes, the reparametrization used to fit many allometric traits: raw traits are usually dominated by a single size gradient, so their genetic covariance is a long, thin ridge that is slow to sample. Size and shape span the same space, so nothing is lost, but the sampler works on well-separated axes.

Usage

size_shape(Y, n_shape = NULL)

Arguments

Y

Numeric matrix of traits, individuals in rows and traits in columns. Log-transformed measurements are the usual input. Missing values (NA) are allowed and are not discarded: see Details.

n_shape

Number of shape axes to keep, between 1 and ncol(Y) - 1, and no more than the numerical rank of the centered shape data. The default requests all ncol(Y) - 1 axes and errors if the data cannot identify them; choose fewer explicitly in that case. Keeping all axes makes the transformation a bijection; fewer axes give a lower-rank (singular) covariance in the original trait space.

Value

A list of class size_shape with

scores

matrix with the size and shape scores, one column each, named size, shape1, shape2, ...;

loadings

ncol(Y) by 1 + n_shape matrix B such that, up to a constant absorbed by the model intercepts, Y = scores %*% t(B);

traits

names of the model traits (size, shape1, ...);

raw_traits

names of the original traits;

centre

column means removed from the shape axes;

gaps

number of entries that were not measured, and so were completed before the transformation (0 for a complete response);

scores_sd

standard deviation of each completed score, on the same layout as scores, or NULL when nothing was completed. Observed individuals have 0.

Details

Size is the mean of the traits, rowMeans(Y), i.e. the log geometric mean for log measurements. Shape is Y - size, which sums to zero within each individual and therefore lives in an ncol(Y) - 1 dimensional subspace; its principal components are the shape axes. Size is often close to the leading axis of variation of a morphometric data set, but it need not be: it is the unweighted mean of the traits, while the principal components are shaped by their covariance structure. The shape axes are ordered by the residual variance they explain. Their numerical rank is at most min(nrow(Y) - 1, ncol(Y) - 1) and can be smaller if the shape data are collinear. It is computed after completing missing values, using a relative singular-value tolerance of max(dim(Y)) * .Machine$double.eps.

The transformation is linear, so genetic and residual covariance matrices transform as \(B M B^T\); use back_transform to do this for the draws of a fit. Signs of the shape axes are arbitrary.

The prior is not invariant under this change of traits, and that is usually an asset. The LKJ prior that lmm_animal puts on the correlation matrix acts on correlations between size and shape instead of correlations between raw traits. The shape axes are principal components of Y - size, so they are uncorrelated in the sample and their genetic correlations are expected to be small; a larger lkj_prior than for the same traits fitted raw (stronger shrinkage towards zero correlation) is therefore reasonable, and it can also make the model cheaper to sample.

Missing values. Size is a mean of all the traits and shape is a difference between them, so a row with a gap has neither. The gap is therefore filled first: the mean and covariance of the traits are estimated by maximum likelihood from the values that were measured (an EM fit of a multivariate normal, which needs no other information), and a missing entry is replaced by its conditional mean given the traits that individual does have. The rest of the transformation then runs unchanged, which is exact for the observed values and a conditional estimate for the completed ones.

Because those completed scores are estimates, scores_sd reports the standard deviation each one carries, and it is worth reading before comparing a mouse that was missing a trait with one that was not: an entry completed from a single measured trait is mostly the model's prediction. A row with nothing observed carries no information and is an error, and two traits never measured on the same individual make their covariance unidentifiable, which is also an error. The EM fit starts from a positive-definite diagonal covariance and errors if it fails to converge or produces a singular covariance. Check the missingness pattern, collinearity and sample size in that case.

The completion is a point estimate, not a multiple imputation: the scores are then treated as data by the model they are passed to, and the uncertainty in scores_sd does not travel into that fit. It is the transformation that is estimated once, exactly as it is for a complete response.

See also

back_transform, animal_design, imputed_data

Examples

set.seed(1)
G <- random_covariance(3, method = "factor", integration = 0.8)
Y <- matrix(rnorm(30 * 3), 30, 3) %*% chol(G)
colnames(Y) <- c("a", "b", "c")
ss <- size_shape(Y)
head(ss$scores)
#>            size       shape1      shape2
#> [1,]  1.4713091 -0.174043125  0.09388516
#> [2,] -0.1054167 -0.527625904  0.23599427
#> [3,] -0.8306718 -0.001639013  0.13899487
#> [4,]  0.1249348 -0.625704797 -0.20420978
#> [5,]  0.8642806  0.270603383  0.34168101
#> [6,]  0.8045399  0.168324928 -0.19979879
ss$loadings
#>   size        PC1        PC2
#> a    1 -0.7464609  0.3308517
#> b    1  0.0867045 -0.8118799
#> c    1  0.6597564  0.4810283

# a gap in one trait is completed from the other two
Y[2, "b"] <- NA
size_shape(Y)$scores[2, ]
#>         size       shape1       shape2 
#>  0.017864835 -0.499582949 -0.000827619
